title: Hillel's seven rules
hookLine: Hillel's rules for reading Torah, later expanded to thirteen

cards: The day before Passover falls on Shabbat, and the leaders of the day, the sons of Bathyra, are stuck. They can't remember whether the Passover offering pushes aside the rules of Shabbat.
Someone mentions a newcomer up from Babylonia, a student of the great teachers of the age. They send for him. His name is Hillel.
He walks in and starts reasoning: a bridge from a shared word, a light-and-heavy argument, one move after another. They aren't moved. Then he says one more sentence, and everything changes.

teach.b: Hillel's seven rules. You met Hillel back in year one; today, his toolbox. The Tosefta, an early collection beside the Mishnah, says Hillel expounded seven rules of reading before the sons of Bathyra.
Two you already know: light and heavy, and the same word.

teach.h: LEARN A THING FROM ITS CONTEXT.
teach.b: Others build a general principle from one verse, or from two; read a general statement together with its particulars; compare a case to a similar one elsewhere; and learn a thing from its context.
Take that last one, because it's easy to feel. The Ten Commandments say, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation, "Thou shalt not steal." Ordinary theft is forbidden elsewhere in the Torah.
So what is this line doing here? Look at its neighbors: murder and adultery, crimes the Torah treats as capital. The Talmud reads it from its context as stealing a person, kidnapping.
Same line, read by the company it keeps. Now the rest of the story. In the Jerusalem Talmud's telling, Hillel's arguments don't move the sons of Bathyra.

teach.h: WHAT I HEARD FROM MY TEACHERS.
teach.b: Then he says: this is what I heard from my teachers, Shemaya and Avtalyon. And they accept him, and make him their leader.
Yesterday's limit, lived out: the rules matter, and so does the chain of teachers they come down through.
Later comes a longer list: a teaching at the start of the Sifra gives Rabbi Ishmael's thirteen rules, with Hillel's tools among them.
Some traditional prayer books print that list in the morning service, so the tools of reading sit right beside the prayers.

how: Some traditional prayer books print Rabbi Ishmael's thirteen rules for reading Torah in the morning service, and students of rabbinic literature learn to recognize each rule as it appears in the Talmud and midrash.

games.q: you're Hillel. you've given the sons of Bathyra a shared-word argument and a light-and-heavy argument, and they still won't accept your answer. what do you say?
o: give them a third, cleverer argument.
this is what I heard from my teachers, Shemaya and Avtalyon.
walk out and go back to Babylonia.
games.why: in the Jerusalem Talmud's telling, naming his teachers is what moves them, and they make him their leader. the rules and the chain of teachers go together.

practice: Bring back one sentence someone said to you recently that stung or puzzled you, and hold the words alone for a moment. Then widen the frame: what came right before it, and what kind of day were they having?
Notice whether the sentence changes when it has its neighbors back.

wordCard.voice: Hillel's seven rules. Seven ways of reading Torah that the Tosefta credits to Hillel, from light and heavy to learning from context, later built on by Rabbi Ishmael's thirteen. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: Hillel, the sage the Tosefta credits with seven rules for reading Torah.

carryVoice: Your line: rules for reading. The tools and the teachers came down together. Until tomorrow.
